sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: O Bromius, because of you I have countless toils
now, and when in youth my body was strong:
first, when, driven mad by Hera,
you left the mountain Nymphs, your nurses, and went away;
then, in the battle of the spear against the Earthborn,
standing at your right foot as your shield-bearer,
I struck Enceladus in the middle of his shield with my spear
and killed him—come, let me see, am I telling of something I saw in a dream?
No, by Zeus, since I even showed the spoils to Bacchus.
And now I am draining to the end a toil greater than those.
For when Hera stirred up against you a Tyrrhenian race
of pirates, so that you might be sold off far away,
I, having learned of it, set sail with my children
in search of you. And on the top of the stern
I myself took hold of the double-oared ship and steered it,
while my sons, sitting at the oars, whitening the grey sea
with their foaming strokes, searched for you, lord.
But when we had already sailed near Malea,
an east wind, blowing upon the ship,
cast us out onto this rock of Aetna,
where the one-eyed sons of the sea god,
the man-slaying Cyclopes, dwell in lonely caves.
Caught by one of these, we are in his house
as slaves; and they call him whom we serve
Polyphemus; and instead of Bacchic revels with their cries of euhoi
we shepherd the flocks of an unholy Cyclops.
My sons, then, on the farthest slopes
pasture the young sheep, being young themselves,
while I, to fill the troughs and sweep the dwelling,
have been posted to remain here, for this impious
Cyclops the servant of his unholy meals.
And now, as I was ordered, I am compelled
to sweep the house with this iron rake,
so that we may receive both my absent master, the Cyclops,
and his sheep in clean caves.
But already I see my sons driving forward
the flocks. What is this? Surely the beat of the sikinnis dance
is not the same for you now as when, with Bacchus,
as revel bands fighting at his side, to the house of Althaea
you went, swaggering to the songs of lyres?

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Child of noble fathers
and of noble mothers,
where, pray, are you going off to the crags?
Is there not here a sheltered breeze
and grassy pasture?
And does not the eddying water of the rivers
lie in the troughs near the ca-
ves? Do you not hear the bleating of your young?

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: —Shoo! Not this way? Will you not graze here,
on the dewy slope?
Hey, I'll throw a stone at you soon
—get along, get along, you horned one—
to the stall-keeper who tends the sheep,
the country-roaming Cyclops.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Loosen your swelling udders;
receive at your teats the offspring
that you leave in the lambs' chambers.
They miss you, they who sleep all day,
the bleating little young ones.
When will you come into the fold,
leaving the grassy pastures,
inside the crags of Aetna?

l.sic: —Shoo! Not this way? Will you not graze here
Hey, I'll throw a stone at you soon
—get along, get along, you horned one—
to the stall-keeper who tends the sheep,

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Here is no Bromius, here are no dances
and thyrsus-bearing Bacchants,
no loud cries of drums
beside gushing springs,
no fresh drops of wine;
nor in Nysa with the Nymphs
do I sing the song "Iacchus, Iacchus"
to Aphrodite,
whom I flew in pursuit of
together with white-footed Bacchants.
O friend!
O dear Bacchus, where do you roam alone?
Where are you tossing your golden hair?
While I, your attendant,
serve as a hired man to the Cyclops,
the one-eyed one, a wandering slave,
in this wretched goatskin cloak,
parted from your friendship.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: Be silent, children, and into the rock-roofed caves
order the servants to gather the flocks.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Go! But what is your hurry, father?

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: I see by the shore the hull of a Greek ship,
and masters of the oar with some commander
coming to this cave; around their necks
they carry empty vessels, in need of food,
and water pitchers. O wretched strangers,
who can they be? They do not know what our master,
Polyphemus, is like, having set foot in this inhospitable
dwelling and having come to the Cyclopean jaw,
the man-eating one, to their misfortune.
But keep quiet, so that we may find out
from where they have come to the Sicilian crag of Aetna.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Strangers, could you tell us of a river stream from which
we might get a cure for thirst, and whether anyone is willing
to sell food to sailors in need?
--What is this? We seem to have come upon a city of Bromius:
I see this throng of Satyrs by the caves.
First I bid the eldest greetings.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: Greetings, stranger; tell me who you are and what your fatherland is.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Odysseus of Ithaca, lord of the land of the Cephallenians.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: I know the man, a shrill rattle, offspring of Sisyphus.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: I am that very man; but do not abuse me.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: From where have you come, sailing to this Sicily?

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: From Ilium, and from the toils of Troy.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: How? Did you not know the passage to your fatherland?

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Storms of wind snatched me here by force.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: Alas! You are enduring the same fortune as I.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Were you too driven here by force?

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: Yes, pursuing the pirates who carried off Bromius.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: What land is this, and who dwell in it?

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: The hill of Aetna, the highest in Sicily.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: And where are the walls and the towers of a city?

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: There are none; the headlands are empty of men, stranger.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: And who hold the land? A race of wild beasts?

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: Cyclopes, who have caves, not roofed houses.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Obeying whom? Or is power in the hands of the people?

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: They are nomads; no one obeys anyone in anything.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Do they sow—or on what do they live?—the grain of Demeter?

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: On milk and cheeses and the flesh of sheep.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: And do they have the drink of Bromius, the streams of the vine?

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: Not at all; and so the land they dwell in is without dancing.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: And are they hospitable and god-fearing toward strangers?

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: Strangers, they say, carry the sweetest meat.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: What do you say? They delight in man-slaying food?

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: No one has come here who was not slaughtered.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: And the Cyclops himself, where is he? Inside his house?

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: Gone off to Aetna, tracking wild beasts with his dogs.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Do you know, then, what to do, so that we may get away from the land?

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: I do not know, Odysseus; but we would do anything for you.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Sell us grain, which we are short of.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: There is nothing, as I said, except meat.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Well, even this is a pleasant check on hunger.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: There is also cheese curdled with fig juice, and cow's milk.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Bring them out; daylight is fitting for goods for sale.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: And you, tell me, how much gold will you give in return?

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Not gold, but I bring the drink of Dionysus.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: O dearest of words! We have long been short of that.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Indeed, Maron gave me the drink, the son of the god.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: He whom I once reared in these arms of mine?

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: The son of Bacchus, so that you may know more clearly.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: Is it in the ship's hold, or do you carry it with you?

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Here is the skin that holds it, as you see, old man.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: That would not even fill my jaw.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Yes;
for there is twice as much drink as can flow out of the skin.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: A fine spring you speak of, and a sweet one for me.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Do you want me to give you a taste of the unmixed wine first?

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: That's fair; for a taste indeed invites the purchase.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Indeed, I also bring along a cup with the skin.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: Come, splash it out, so that I may remember by drinking.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: There.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: Oh my, what a fine smell it has!

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: What, did you see it?

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: No, by Zeus, but I smell it.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Taste it now, so that you do not praise it in word only.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: Wow! Bacchus is calling me to dance.
Ah, ah, ah!

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Did it not gurgle nicely down your throat?

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: So that it reached right to the tips of my nails.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Besides this, however, we will also give you money.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: Just loosen the skin; let the gold be.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Bring out the cheeses now, or the young of the sheep.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: I will do it, caring little for my masters.
For I would be mad enough, to drink a single cup,
to give in exchange the flocks of all the Cyclopes,
and to throw myself into the brine from the Leucadian rock,
once I was drunk and had let my brows relax.
For whoever does not rejoice when he drinks is mad;
in drinking one can make this thing here stand up straight,
and grab a breast, and touch with both hands
a meadow made ready, and there is dancing as well
and forgetfulness of troubles. Shall I then not kiss
such a drink, and tell the stupidity of the Cyclops
to go hang, and the eye in the middle of his head as well?

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Listen, Odysseus; let us have a little chat with you.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Indeed, you approach as friends to a friend.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Did you take Troy, and Helen into your hands?

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Yes, and we sacked the whole house of the sons of Priam.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Well then, when you had taken the young woman,
did you not all bang her in turn,
since she does like to be married to many?
The traitress! Seeing the embroidered breeches
around his two legs, and the golden
collar he wore around the middle of his neck,
she was all aflutter, and left Menelaus, a most excellent
little fellow, behind. Would that the race of women
had never been born anywhere — except for me alone.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: Look, here for you are the herdsmen's beasts,
lord Odysseus, nurslings of bleating lambs,
and no scanty cheeses of curdled milk.
Carry them off; go away from the caves as fast as you can,
giving me in exchange the drink of the Bacchic grape.
—Alas! Here comes the Cyclops; what shall we do?

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Then we are done for, old man; where should we flee?

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: Inside this rock, where you may escape notice.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: A terrible thing you have said, to go into the nets.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: Not terrible; there are many refuges in the rock.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: No indeed; for Troy would groan greatly
if we flee from one man, when a countless throng
of Phrygians I often withstood with my shield.
No, if we must die, we will die nobly,
or, if we live, we will keep our former fame safe as well.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: Up! Make way! What is this? What is this idleness?
Why are you playing the Bacchant? This is no Dionysus here,
no rattles of bronze or clashing of drums.
How are my newborn young in the caves?
Are they at the teats, and do they run beneath their mothers'
sides? And in the rush baskets
is there a full supply of cheeses milked out?
What do you say? What are you telling me? Soon one of you, thanks to my club,
will shed tears; look up and not down.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: There, we have tilted our heads back toward Zeus himself,
and I see the stars and Orion.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: Is my breakfast well prepared?

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: It is here. Only let your gullet be ready.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: And are the mixing bowls full of milk too?

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: So full that you can drink off a whole jar, if you like.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: Sheep's milk or cow's or mixed?

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Whichever you want; only don't swallow me down.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: Not at all; for in the middle of my belly
you would kill me with your leaping, with your dance figures.
Ha! What is this throng I see by the folds?
Have some pirates or thieves put in to the land?
I do see these lambs from my caves
with their bodies bound together with twisted withies,
and the cheese baskets in disorder, and the old man
with his bald face swollen from blows.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: Ah me, I am in a fever, wretch that I am, beaten all over.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: By whom? Who has been boxing your head, old man?

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: By these men, Cyclops, because I would not let them carry off your things.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: Did they not know that I am a god and born of gods?

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: I told them so; but they kept carrying off the goods;
and the cheese, though I tried to stop them, they ate,
and they carried the lambs out; and after binding you
in a three-cubit collar, and then your eye in the middle
they said they would tear out your guts by force,
and flay your back well with a whip,
and then, after tying you up and throwing you onto the rowing benches
of the ship, they would sell you to someone
to heave stones, or throw you into a mill.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: Really? Then won't you go as fast as you can
and sharpen the cleavers and knives, and put a great bundle of wood
on the fire and light it? For they will be slaughtered at once
and fill my belly, as I eat straight from the coals
a hot meal, I who carve the meat,
and the rest boiled and stewed from the cauldron.
For I am glutted with mountain food;
I have had enough of feasting on lions
and deer, and it is long since I have had a meal of men.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: New things, after the usual ones, master,
are sweeter. For indeed not recently
have other strangers come to your caves.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Cyclops, hear the strangers too in turn.
We, in need of food, to make a purchase
came near your caves from our ship.
And the lambs, for a cup of wine, this man
sold us and handed them over, after he had taken a drink,
willing to willing buyers, and none of it was done by force.
But there is nothing sound in what this man says,
since he was caught selling your goods behind your back.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: I? Yes, may you perish miserably—

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: if I am lying.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: By Poseidon who begot you, O Cyclops,
by great Triton and by Nereus,
by Calypso and the daughters of Nereus,
and the holy waves and the whole race of fish,
I swear, O most handsome, O dear little Cyclops,
O little master, that I was not selling your
goods to the strangers. Or else may these wicked
children perish wickedly, whom I love most of all.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Keep that for yourself. I myself saw you selling the goods
to the strangers; and if I speak falsely,
may my father perish; but do not wrong the strangers.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: You lie; I for my part trust this man more
than Rhadamanthys, and I say he is more just.
But I want to ask: from where did you sail, strangers?
From what country? What city brought you up?

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: We are Ithacans by birth, and from Ilium,
after sacking the city, driven by sea winds
to your land we have come, Cyclops.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: Are you the ones who went after the rape of the most wicked
Helen, to the city of Ilium, neighbour of the Scamander?

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: We are, having endured that terrible toil to the end.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: A shameful expedition, you who for the sake of one
woman sailed out to the land of the Phrygians.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: The matter was a god's doing; blame none of the mortals.
But we, O noble son of the sea god,
both supplicate you and speak frankly:
do not bring yourself to kill friends who have come to your caves
and to make them impious food for your jaws;
for it was we who, lord, saved for your father his temple seats,
to keep them, in the recesses of the land of Hellas.
The holy harbour of Taenarus remains unbroken,
and the farthest hiding places of Malea, and the rock of Sunium,
sacred to divine Athena, safe, with its silver beneath,
and the refuges of Geraestus; and of Hellas

l.sic: the grievous disgraces we did not give to the Phrygians;

sp.l: and in this you too have a share; for in the recesses of the land of Hellas
you dwell, under Aetna, the fire-dripping rock.
And there is a law for mortals, if you turn away from my arguments:
to receive suppliants ruined at sea,
and to give them gifts of hospitality and help them with clothes,
not to fix their limbs on ox-piercing
spits and fill your belly and jaw with them.
The land of Priam has bereaved Hellas enough,
drinking the spear-shed blood of many dead,
and it has destroyed wives without husbands, old women without children
and grey-haired fathers. But if those who are left
you roast and consume in a bitter feast,
where will one turn? But be persuaded by me, Cyclops:
let go the greed of your jaw, and piety
choose instead of impiety; for to many
wicked gains have brought punishment in return.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: I want to give you some advice: of the meat
of this man leave nothing, and if you bite his tongue,
you will become clever and most talkative, Cyclops.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: Wealth, little man, is the god for the wise;
the rest is boasting and fine-sounding words.
The sea headlands on which my father has his shrines
I bid farewell; why did you put these forward in your speech?
The thunderbolt of Zeus I do not shudder at, stranger,
nor do I know in what way Zeus is a mightier god than I.
I do not care about him for the future; and why I do not care,
listen. When he pours rain down from above,
in this rock, having a watertight shelter,
on a roast calf or some wild beast
feasting, and drenching my upturned belly well,
drinking a jar of milk on top of it, my robe
I beat, thundering in rivalry with the thunder of Zeus.
And when the Thracian north wind pours down snow,
wrapping my body in the skins of beasts
and kindling a fire—I care nothing for snow.
And the earth, of necessity, whether it wants to or not,
bearing grass, fattens my flocks.
These I sacrifice to no one but myself, and not to the gods,
and to the greatest of deities, this belly here.
For to drink and to eat day by day,
that is Zeus for sensible men,
and to cause oneself no grief. As for those who laid down
the laws, complicating the life of men,
I tell them to go weep; and my own soul I
shall not stop treating well—by eating you up.
And you will get gifts of hospitality such as these, so that I may be blameless:
fire, and this ancestral cauldron here, which, boiling,
will nicely wrap your flesh, torn to pieces.
But creep inside, so that, to the god of the fold,
standing around the altar, you may give me a good feast.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Alas, I escaped the toils of Troy
and of the sea, but now on the mind of an unholy man
I have run aground, and on his harbourless heart.
O Pallas, O mistress, Zeus-born goddess,
now, now help! For toils greater than those of Ilium
I have come to, and to the very brink of danger.
And you who dwell in the seats of the shining stars,
Zeus, god of strangers, look on this; for if you do not see it,
you are wrongly held to be Zeus, being a god of no account.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Of your wide gullet, O Cyclops,
open wide the lip; for ready for you
are boiled things and roasted things and, from the coals,
to gnaw, to chew,
to carve up the limbs of strangers,
as you recline on a shaggy goatskin.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Don't, don't give me any;
alone, by yourself, load the hull of your boat.
Farewell to this dwelling,
and farewell to the victims,
the altarless sacrifice that he holds,
the Cyclops of Aetna, who in foreign
flesh takes delight as his food.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Pitiless, O wretch, is he who from his home
sacrifices the foreign suppliants at his hearth, from his house,
feasting on them boiled, and with abominable teeth
cutting, chewing
the hot flesh of men from the coals,

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Don't, don't give me any;
alone, by yourself, load the hull of your boat.
Farewell to this dwelling,
and farewell to the victims,
the altarless sacrifice that he holds,
the Cyclops of Aetna, who in foreign
flesh takes delight as his food.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: O Zeus, what am I to say, having seen terrible things inside the cave,
things not to be believed, like tales, and not like the deeds of mortals?

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: What is it, Odysseus? Surely the most unholy Cyclops
has not feasted on your dear comrades?

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Yes, on two, after looking them over and weighing them in his hands,
men who had the best-fed thickness of flesh.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: How, poor man, did you fare while suffering this?

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: When to this rocky land we came,
he first kindled a fire, throwing trunks
of a lofty oak onto his broad hearth,
a load fit for three wagons to carry.
Then, of fir branches, on the ground
he spread a bed near the flame of the fire.
And he filled a mixing bowl holding about ten amphoras,
having milked the cows, pouring in the white milk.
And he set beside it a cup of ivy-wood, three
cubits in breadth, and it looked four deep.
And he set a bronze cauldron boiling on the fire,
and spits, their tips hardened in the fire,
and the rest smoothed with a sickle, made of branches of thorn,

l.sic: and Aetnaean basins for the slaughter by the jaws of axes.

sp.l: And when everything was ready for the god-hated
cook of Hades, he seized two men
of my comrades and slaughtered them, and with one rhythm
he threw the one into the bronze-beaten hollow of the cauldron,
and the other, seizing him by the tendon at the end of his foot,
and striking him against a sharp point of rocky stone,
he dashed out his brains; and cutting away
the flesh with a fierce knife, he roasted it in the fire,
and the limbs he put into the cauldron to boil.
And I, wretched man, shedding tears from my eyes,
came close to the Cyclops and waited on him;
the others, like birds in the recesses of the rock,
cowered, and there was no blood in their skin.
But when, sated with the flesh of my comrades,
he fell back, sending out a heavy breath from his gullet,
something divine came into my mind: filling a cup
with this wine of Maron, I offer it to him to drink,
saying this: O Cyclops, son of the sea god,
see what a divine drink Hellas brings
from her vines, this gladness of Dionysus.
And he, being full of his shameless food,
took it and drained it, gulping it down at one draught,
and praised it, raising his hand: Dearest of strangers,
it is a fine drink you give me on top of a fine feast.
And when I perceived that he was pleased,
I gave him another cup, knowing that
the wine would wound him and he would soon pay the penalty.
And indeed he was moving on to songs. And I, pouring in
one cup after another, kept heating his guts with the drink.
And he is singing, beside my weeping shipmates,
unmusical songs, and the cave echoes. And I came out
in silence. You and myself I wish to save, if you are willing.
But tell me whether you wish or do not wish
to flee a savage man, and in the halls of Bacchus
to dwell with the Danaid nymphs.
For your father, inside, has agreed to this.
But he is weak and is helping himself to the drink,
and, as if caught by the cup as by birdlime,
he is flapping his wings; but you—for you are young—
save yourself with me, and take back your old friend
Dionysus, who is not like the Cyclops.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: O dearest friend, if only we might see this day,
escaping the unholy head of the Cyclops.
For it is a long time indeed that our dear siphon

l.sic: we have been bereft of. —And we have none to gulp down.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Hear now what punishment I have
for the villainous beast, and what escape from your slavery.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Speak, for we would not more gladly hear the sound of an Asian
lyre than news that the Cyclops has perished.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: He wants to go revelling to his brothers,
the Cyclopes, delighted with this drink of Bacchus.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: I understand: catching him alone in the thickets
you mean to slaughter him, or push him down from the rocks.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Nothing of the sort; what I have in mind is a trick.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: How then? We have long heard that you are clever.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: To keep him away from this revel, telling him
that he must not give this drink to the Cyclopes,
but keep it for himself alone and live his life pleasantly.
And when he falls asleep, overcome by Bacchus,
there is a branch of olive in the house,
which I, sharpening its tip with this sword,
will put into the fire; and then, when, burning,
I see it, I will lift it and thrust it hot into the middle
of the Cyclops' face, and melt his eye out with fire.
And as a man fitting together the timbers of a ship
works a drill with a double strap,
so will I whirl the brand in the light-bearing
eye of the Cyclops and burn up his pupil.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Hurrah, hurrah!
I rejoice, we are mad with joy at your inventions.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: And then you and your friends and the old man,
putting you aboard the hollow hull of my black ship,
I will send away from this land with double oars.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Is there a way, then, as if at a libation to the god,
that I too might take hold of the eye-blinding
brand? For I want to share in this killing.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: You must indeed; for the brand is big; you must all take hold of it.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: I would even lift the load of a hundred wagons,
if of the Cyclops, who will die a miserable death,
we shall smoke out the eye like a wasps' nest.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Be silent now; for you know the trick well;
and when I give the order, the master builders
obey. For I will not abandon my friends
who are inside and be saved alone.
And yet I could flee, and I have got out of the recesses of the cave;
but it is not just to abandon my friends,
with whom I came here, and be saved alone.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Come, who will be first, and who, posted after the first,
grasping the handle of the brand,
and thrusting it inside the eyelids of the Cyclops,
will grind out his bright eye?
Hush, hush. For look, drunk,
making a graceless din of music,
a clumsy singer and soon to weep,
he comes out of his rocky halls.
Come, let us teach him with our revel songs,
this untaught one;
in any case he is going to be blind.

sp.speaker: Semichor. Chorus
sp.l: Blessed is he who cries euhoi
at the dear springs of the grape clusters,
spreading his wings for the revel,
embracing a dear friend,
and on a couch holding the golden
of a dainty mistress,
anointed with myrrh, the glistening lo-
ck, and he says: Who will open the door for me?

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: Papapa! I am full of wine,
and I rejoice in the bloom of the feast,
loaded like a merchant ship's hull
up to the deck at the top of my belly.
The cheerful fodder leads me on
to revel in the season of spring
with my brothers the Cyclopes.
Come, stranger, come, hand me the skin.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Gazing beautifully from his eyes,
the beautiful one comes forth from his halls.
— Papapa! Somebody loves us.–-
And blazing torches await your
body, and like a tender bride
from within the dewy caves.
And garlands of more than one colour
will soon keep company with your head.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Cyclops, listen: for with this Bacchus
whom I gave you to drink I am well acquainted.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: And what sort of god is Bacchus held to be?

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: The greatest for men, for the enjoyment of life.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: I certainly belch him up with pleasure.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Such is the god: he harms no mortal.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: But how can a god be happy having his home in a wineskin?

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Wherever one puts him, there he is content.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: Gods ought not to keep their bodies in skins.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: What of it, if he delights you? Or is the skin bitter to you?

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: I hate the skin; but this drink I love.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Stay here, then, and drink and be merry, Cyclops.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: Should I not give my brothers a share of this drink?

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: If you keep it yourself, you will appear more honoured.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: But if I give it to my friends, more useful.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Revelling loves fistfights and abusive quarrels.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: I am drunk, but all the same no one would touch me.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: My good man, one who has been drinking should stay at home.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: A fool is he who drinks and does not love revelling.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: But whoever stays at home when he is drunk is wise.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: What shall we do, Silenus? Do you think we should stay?

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: I do. For what need is there of other drinking companions, Cyclops?

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: And indeed the ground is soft with flowering grass . . . .

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: And besides, it is good to drink in the warmth of the sun.
Lie down now for me, putting your side on the ground.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: There.
Why, then, are you putting the mixing bowl behind me?

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: So that no one passing by may knock it over.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: No, it is to drink
on the sly that you want; put it down in the middle.
And you, stranger, tell me the name by which I should call you.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Nobody; and what favour shall I receive, so that I may praise you?

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: I shall feast on you last of all your comrades.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: A fine privilege you give your guest, Cyclops.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: You there, what are you doing? Are you drinking up the wine on the sly?

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: No, but it kissed me, because I am good-looking.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: You will weep for loving the wine that does not love you.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: Yes it does, by Zeus, since it says it loves me because I am handsome.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: Pour, and make the cup full. Just give it to me.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: Well, how has it been mixed? Come, let us check.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: You will be the death of me; give it as it is.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: No, by Zeus, not before I
see you take a garland and have another taste . . .

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: O unjust wine-pourer!

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: No, by Zeus, but O sweet wine!
You must wipe your nose so as to get a drink.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: There, my lip is clean, and my beard.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: Now set your elbow gracefully, and then drink it off,
just as you see me drinking—and as you do not see me.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: Ah, ah, what are you doing?

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: I took a pleasant swig.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: Take it, stranger, and be my wine-pourer yourself.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: The vine is at any rate familiar to my hand.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: Come, pour now.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: I am pouring; just be quiet.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: That is a hard thing you have said, to one who drinks a lot.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: There, take it and drink it off and leave nothing.
One must drain it and die along with the drink.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: Wow, how clever is the wood of the vine!

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: And if you drain a lot of it after a big meal,
soaking your belly till it is not thirsty, it will put you to sleep,
but if you leave anything, Bacchus will dry you out.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: Hurrah, hurrah,
how hard it was to swim out! Unmixed is the pleasure.
The sky seems to me to be mixed together
with the earth and to be whirling round, and the throne of Zeus
I see, and the whole holy majesty of the gods.
—I would not kiss you!—The Graces are tempting me.—
With this Ganymede here I shall take my rest well enough,
most beautifully, by the Graces. —Somehow I take more pleasure
in boys than in females.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: What, am I Zeus's Ganymede, Cyclops?

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: Yes, by Zeus, the one I am carrying off from Dardanus.

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: I am done for, children; I shall suffer cruel evils.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: Do you find fault with your lover and play coy with him because he is drunk?

sp.speaker: Silenus
sp.l: Ah me! I shall soon find the wine most bitter.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Come now, sons of Dionysus, noble children,
the man is inside; and, relaxed in sleep,
he will soon spew meat out of his shameless gullet.
And the brand inside the cave, pushing out smoke,
is made ready; and nothing remains but to burn
the Cyclops' eye; but see that you are a man.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: We will have a spirit of rock and adamant.
But go into the house, before our father suffers something
desperate; for things here are ready for you.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Hephaestus, lord of Aetna, burn out the bright eye
of your evil neighbour and be rid of him once and for all,
and you, Sleep, nursling of black Night,
come in full force upon the god-hated beast,
and do not, after the most glorious toils of Troy,
destroy Odysseus himself and his sailors
at the hands of a man who cares nothing for gods or mortals.
Or else we must believe that chance is a god,
and that the power of the gods is less than chance.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: It will seize the throat
tightly, the crab-claw tongs,
of the guest-devourer; for soon with fire
it will destroy his light-bearing pupils.
Already
the brand, turned to charcoal,
is hidden in the ashes, the huge
sapling of oak; but let Maron come;
let him do his work;
let him take out the eye of the raving Cy-
clops, so that he may rue his drinking.
And I
the ivy-loving Bromius, the de-
sired one, wish to behold,
from the Cy-
clops' solitude departing;
will I ever come so far?

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Be silent, by the gods, you beasts, keep quiet,
closing the joints of your mouths; I allow no one even to breathe,
or to blink, or to clear his throat,
so that the evil thing is not woken, until the sight
of the Cyclops' eye has been forced out by fire.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: We are silent, gulping down the air in our jaws.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Come now, see that you take hold of the brand with your hands
when you go inside; it is nicely red-hot.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Then won't you assign who must be first
to take the burning bar and burn out the light
of the Cyclops, so that we may share in the fortune?

sp.speaker: Chorus A
sp.l: We are standing too far away in front of the doors
to push the fire into his eye.

sp.speaker: Chorus B
sp.l: And we have just now gone lame.

sp.speaker: Chorus C
sp.l: Then you have suffered the same as I; for our feet
got sprained while we were standing, I don't know how.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Sprained while standing?

sp.speaker: Chorus D
sp.l: And our eyes, too,
are full of dust or ash from somewhere.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Worthless men, and no allies at all, these.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Because we pity our back and our spine,
and I do not want to have my teeth knocked out
by being beaten, is that cowardice?
But I know a spell of Orpheus, a very good one,
so that the brand, going of its own accord into the skull,
sets fire to the one-eyed son of Earth.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: I knew long ago that you were like this by nature,
and now I know it better. My own friends
I must use. But if you have no strength in your hands,
then at least cheer us on, so that we may gain courage
from the urging of you, our friends.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: I will do it. We will run the risk with the Carian.
And as far as our cheering goes, let the Cyclops be smoked.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Io, io! Most nobly pu-
sh, hurry. Burn out the brow
of the guest-devouring beast.
Smoke him out, burn
the shepherd of Aetna.
Twist it, drag it, lest, maddened with pain,
he does something rash to you.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: Ah me, the light of my eye has been burnt to a cinder.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: A fine paean indeed; sing it for me, O Cyclops.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: Ah me, ah me, how I have been outraged, how I am undone!
But you shall certainly not escape out of this rock
to rejoice, you nobodies; for at the entrance
of the cleft I will stand and fit these hands of mine into it.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Why are you shouting, Cyclops?

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: I am ruined.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: You do look ugly.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: And wretched besides.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Did you fall into the middle of the coals while drunk?

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: Nobody has ruined me.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Then nobody was wronging you.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: Nobody is blinding my eye.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Then you are not blind.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: As if you—

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: And how could nobody make you blind?

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: You mock me. But where is Nobody?

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Nowhere, Cyclops.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: It was the stranger, so that you may understand correctly, who ruined me,
the villain, who gave me the drink and swamped me.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Yes, wine is terrible and hard to wrestle with.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: By the gods, have they fled, or are they staying inside the house?

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: These men are standing in silence, having taken the overhanging rock
as their shelter.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: On which hand?

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: On your right.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: Where?

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Right against the rock.
Have you got them?

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: Evil upon evil; I struck my skull
and broke it.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: And they are escaping you, too.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: Not this way? Didn't you say this way?

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: No; I mean that way.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: Which way, then?

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Turn around, over there, to the left.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: Ah me, I am laughed at; you mock me in my misery.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: But not any more; he is right in front of you.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: O utter villain, where on earth are you?

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Far from you
I keep this body of Odysseus under guard.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: What did you say? You have changed your name and speak a new one.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: The very one my father gave me: Odysseus.
You were bound to pay the penalty for your unholy feast;
for it would have been poor work to burn Troy to the ground
if I had not avenged on you the murder of my comrades.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: Alas! An old oracle is being fulfilled.
For it said that I would have my sight blinded by you
when you set out from Troy. But it also foretold
that you would pay the penalty for this,
tossed about on the sea for a long time.

sp.speaker: Odysseus
sp.l: Go weep, I say; I have already done what you say.
And I will go to the shore, and the hull of my ship
I will launch onto the Sicilian sea and toward my fatherland.

sp.speaker: Cyclops
sp.l: No indeed, for I will break off a piece of this rock
and throw it and crush you, shipmates and all.
I will go up onto the hill, blind though I am,
through this cave with its two openings, climbing on foot.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: And we, being shipmates of this Odysseus,
will serve Bacchus from now on.
